explanation.body: The net force is the centripetal force, $F=mr\omega^2$. The forces on the $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $8.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ masses are $(5.0)(2.0)\omega^2=10\omega^2$ and $(8.0)(6.0)\omega^2=48\omega^2$, respectively. Both masses have the same $\omega$, so the ratio is $10:48=5:24$.

perOption.A: Inverts the ratio obtained by assuming both masses have the same linear speed.
perOption.C: Uses the inverse-radius dependence for equal linear speeds, although the platform fixes the angular speed.
perOption.D: Reverses the order of the two forces.

difficultyReason: The shared angular speed cancels in a direct centripetal-force ratio.
misconception: Assuming the masses share a linear speed.
transcription:
Two objects of masses $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $8.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ are fixed on a horizontal circular platform $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ and $6.0\ \mathrm{m}$ from the centre respectively.

When the platform is rotated with uniform circular motion, what is the ratio of the net force on the $5.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass to the $8.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ mass?

A $8:15$
B $5:24$
C $15:8$
D $24:5$

explanation.body: For a uniform sphere of density $\rho$, the surface field is $g=GM/r^2=(G/r^2)(\rho\,4\pi r^3/3)=(4\pi G\rho/3)r$. Doubling the radius at the same density doubles the surface field to $2X$.

perOption.A: Applies the inverse-square law while holding the mass fixed.
perOption.B: Treats the surface field as inversely proportional to radius at fixed density.
perOption.D: Uses a quadratic dependence on radius, although the mass scales as the cube of the radius.

difficultyReason: The inverse-square law must be combined with how mass scales at fixed density.
misconception: Holding mass fixed when the sphere grows.

explanation.body: A geostationary satellite has a period of $24$ hours. Its orbital speed is $v=r\omega=2\pi r/T=2\pi(6.40\times10^6+3.59\times10^7)/(24\times60\times60)=3.08\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Omits the factor of $2\pi$ in the circumference.
perOption.B: Uses the altitude alone as the orbital radius.
perOption.D: Uses the period in minutes and reports the result in kilometres per second.

difficultyReason: The calculation requires the orbital radius and the period implied by geostationary motion.
misconception: Using altitude as the orbital radius.
transcription:
A communication satellite is in a geostationary orbit at a height of $3.59\times10^7\ \mathrm{m}$ above the equator. The radius of the Earth is $6.40\times10^6\ \mathrm{m}$.

How fast is the satellite travelling?

A $0.490\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$
B $2.60\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$
C $3.08\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$
D $186\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$

explanation.body: The two curves are half a cycle apart. In simple harmonic motion, the acceleration–time and displacement–time graphs are $\pi$ radians out of phase.

perOption.A: Acceleration and velocity are a quarter of a cycle apart.
perOption.C: Displacement and velocity are a quarter of a cycle apart.
perOption.D: Resultant force is in phase with acceleration and a quarter of a cycle from velocity.

difficultyReason: The student must identify a half-cycle phase difference and match it to SHM variables.
misconception: Confusing a quarter-cycle phase shift with a half-cycle shift.

explanation.body: The total energy scales as $E\propto\omega^2x_0^2\propto x_0^2/T^2$, where $x_0$ is the amplitude and $T$ is the period. Thus $E_2/E_1=(T_1/3T_1)^2(2x_{0,1}/x_{0,1})^2=4/9$, giving $E_2=(4/9)(18\ \mathrm{mJ})=8.0\ \mathrm{mJ}$.

perOption.B: Scales the energy by the unsquared ratio $2/3$.
perOption.C: Doubles the energy as if it were proportional to amplitude alone.
perOption.D: Squares the amplitude factor but leaves out the change in period.

difficultyReason: The student must combine the squared amplitude dependence with the inverse-square period dependence.
misconception: Scaling energy linearly with amplitude or period.

explanation.body: The period is $T=1/f=1/5000=0.20\ \mathrm{ms}$. One period spans two horizontal squares ($2\ \mathrm{cm}$), so the time base is $0.20/2=0.10\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}=100\ \mathrm{\mu s\,cm^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: This time base gives only $20\ \mathrm{\mu s}$ across the two squares of one cycle.
perOption.C: This setting gives a period of $20\ \mathrm{ms}$, a factor of 100 too large.
perOption.D: This setting gives a period of $200\ \mathrm{ms}$, a factor of 1000 too large.

difficultyReason: The student converts frequency to period and reads the horizontal length of one cycle.
misconception: Using the whole display width for one period.
transcription:
A cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) is used to display a wave of frequency $5.0\ \mathrm{kHz}$. The display is shown.

[The display shows a sinusoidal trace with five complete cycles across ten horizontal squares on a grid six squares high. Scale arrows show that each square is $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ wide and $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ high.]

What is the time-base setting of the CRO?

A $10\ \mathrm{\mu s\,cm^{-1}}$
B $100\ \mathrm{\mu s\,cm^{-1}}$
C $10\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}$
D $100\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}$

explanation.body: For the position shown, the path difference is $OY-OX=XY$. The waves meet in phase when this is $n\lambda$, with $n$ an integer. With $\lambda=0.75\ \mathrm{m}$, $XY=1.50\ \mathrm{m}$ gives $n=2$.

perOption.A: The path difference is $3.50\ \mathrm{m}$ outside the pair or $1.00\ \mathrm{m}$ between the speakers, neither an integer multiple of the wavelength.
perOption.B: The path difference is $2.75\ \mathrm{m}$ outside the pair or $1.25\ \mathrm{m}$ between the speakers, neither an integer multiple of the wavelength.
perOption.C: The path difference is $2.00\ \mathrm{m}$, which is not an integer multiple of $0.75\ \mathrm{m}$.

issues: The key applies the path-difference formula for the exterior position shown. The stem also permits O between the speakers, but checking those positions gives no additional correct option.
difficultyReason: The student must translate a collinear arrangement into a path difference and test for a whole number of wavelengths.
misconception: Using one source-to-observer distance as the path difference.
transcription:
Two loudspeakers X and Y emit sound waves that are in phase and of wavelength $0.75\ \mathrm{m}$.

An observer O is able to stand anywhere on a straight line that passes through X and Y, as shown. The observer stands at a point where the sound waves from X and Y meet in phase.

[O, X and Y lie on a dashed straight line in that order from left to right.]

What could be the distances OY and XY?

Distance OY / m | Distance XY / m
A $1.25$ | $3.50$
B $2.00$ | $2.75$
C $2.75$ | $2.00$
D $3.25$ | $1.50$

explanation.body: The first diffraction minimum satisfies $\sin\theta=\lambda/b$, where $b$ is the slit width. At small angles this makes the central maximum width proportional to $D\lambda/b$, where $D$ is the slit-to-screen distance, so B, C and D are true. Widening the slit lets more light through and increases the area under the intensity graph, making A the incorrect statement.

perOption.A: Correct. A wider slit increases the area under the graph.
perOption.B: A longer wavelength increases the width of the central maximum, so this statement is true.
perOption.C: A larger slit-to-screen distance increases the width of the central maximum, so this statement is true.
perOption.D: A narrower slit increases the width of the central maximum, so this statement is true.

issues: The key writes $x/D=\lambda/b$ as a small-angle relation. The diagram defines $x$ as the full central maximum width, so $x/D\approx2\lambda/b$. The proportionality and answer are unaffected.
difficultyReason: The student must distinguish changes to the central maximum width from changes to the total transmitted light.
misconception: Assuming a wider slit transmits the same amount of light.

explanation.body: At constant horizontal speed $u$, travelling a horizontal distance $s_x$ takes $t=s_x/u$. The vertical displacement is $s_y=\tfrac12 at^2=\tfrac12 a(s_x/u)^2$, so for constant $a$ and $u$ it is proportional to $s_x^2$. With $p=kx^2=1.0\ \mathrm{mm}$, $q=4p=4.0\ \mathrm{mm}$, $r=9p=9.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ and $s=16p=16.0\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.A: Uses a square-root dependence on horizontal distance.
perOption.B: Uses a linear dependence on horizontal distance.
perOption.C: Doubles the deflection at each equal horizontal interval, assuming exponential growth.

difficultyReason: The student must combine constant horizontal velocity and uniform vertical acceleration to obtain a square law.
misconception: Treating deflection as proportional to horizontal travel.
transcription:
The diagram shows the path of a horizontal beam of electrons passing through the uniform vertical electric field between two horizontal electrodes. The diagram is not to scale.

[The electrons enter from the left at the position marked $0$ and curve upwards between the electrodes. Vertical offsets from the dashed horizontal entry line to the beam are labelled $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$ at horizontal distances $x$, $2x$, $3x$ and $4x$.]

The vertical displacements of the beam after travelling through horizontal distances of $x$, $2x$, $3x$ and $4x$ are represented by $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$.

Which row represents the values of $p$, $q$, $r$ and $s$?

$p/\mathrm{mm}$ | $q/\mathrm{mm}$ | $r/\mathrm{mm}$ | $s/\mathrm{mm}$
A $1.0$ | $1.4$ | $1.7$ | $2.0$
B $1.0$ | $2.0$ | $3.0$ | $4.0$
C $1.0$ | $2.0$ | $4.0$ | $8.0$
D $1.0$ | $4.0$ | $9.0$ | $16.0$

explanation.body: Redraw the ladder so that the two rightmost resistors in series form a branch parallel to the middle vertical resistor. The series branch carries $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$ and drops $2.0\ \mathrm{V}$, so the parallel resistor carries $2.0\ \mathrm{A}$ and the middle top resistor carries $3.0\ \mathrm{A}$. This makes the first vertical branch’s p.d. $5.0\ \mathrm{V}$, so it draws $5.0\ \mathrm{A}$ and the first top resistor carries $8.0\ \mathrm{A}$. The input p.d. is $V=8.0+3.0+2.0=13.0\ \mathrm{V}$.

perOption.A: Counts only the voltage across the two rightmost resistors in series.
perOption.B: Stops at the voltage across the first vertical branch.
perOption.C: Counts only the voltage across the first top resistor.

difficultyReason: The ladder requires alternating voltage and current calculations across two successive junctions.
misconception: Using the end-branch current for all the resistors.
transcription:
A network of resistors, each of resistance $1.0\ \Omega$, is connected as shown.

[The input terminals on the left have potential difference $V$. Three $1.0\ \Omega$ resistors lie along the top rail. After each top resistor, a vertical $1.0\ \Omega$ resistor connects that node to the common bottom rail. The bottom wire from the rightmost branch carries $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$ to the left.]

The current passing through the end resistor is $1.0\ \mathrm{A}$.

What is the potential difference $V$ across the input terminals?

A $2.0\ \mathrm{V}$
B $5.0\ \mathrm{V}$
C $8.0\ \mathrm{V}$
D $13.0\ \mathrm{V}$

explanation.body: The filament lamp’s $I$-against-$V$ graph starts at the origin and flattens as $V$ rises. Swapping the axes reflects the curve across the line that interchanges the axes, giving a $V$-against-$I$ graph that gets steeper as $I$ rises.

perOption.C: Shows a nonzero potential difference at zero current and the wrong curvature.
perOption.D: Uses the flattening shape of the $I$-against-$V$ characteristic with the axes swapped.

difficultyReason: The familiar filament-lamp characteristic must be interpreted with voltage on the vertical axis.
misconception: Keeping the usual current-on-vertical-axis curve after swapping axes.
transcription:
Which graph shows the variation with current $I$ of the potential difference $V$ of a filament lamp?

[All four graphs have $V$ on the vertical axis and $I$ on the horizontal axis.]
A [An increasing curve from the origin that gets steeper.]
B [An increasing straight line through the origin.]
C [An increasing curve that starts at a positive $V$ when $I=0$ and flattens.]
D [An increasing curve from the origin that flattens.]

explanation.body: The branches share the same p.d., so $2I_1=3I_2=4I_3$. The supply current is $I=I_1+I_2+I_3=(3/2)I_2+I_2+(3/4)I_2$, giving $I_2=4I/13$. Substitution gives $I_1=6I/13$ and $I_3=3I/13$, so $I_1:I_2:I_3=6:4:3$.

perOption.A: Reverses the branch-current order, putting the smallest current through the smallest resistance.
perOption.C: Makes current increase with resistance despite the common branch voltage.
perOption.D: Splits the current in descending order but gives unequal branch voltages, since $2(18)\ne3(16)$.

difficultyReason: The equal branch voltages make the current ratio the inverse of the resistance ratio.
misconception: Assigning the largest current to the largest resistance.

explanation.body: The cable carries current into the page and the field lies in the plane of the page, so the angle between them is $90^\circ$. The force is $F=BIL\sin\theta=(4.0\times10^{-5})(3.0)(2.0)\sin90^\circ=240\ \mathrm{\mu N}$.

perOption.A: Uses too small an effective field component even though the entire field is perpendicular to the cable.
perOption.B: Uses $\sin65^\circ$ by taking the field’s inclination to the horizontal as the current–field angle.
perOption.D: Exceeds $BIL$, the maximum possible force for the given field, current and length.

difficultyReason: The calculation is direct once the angle between the current and the field is read in three dimensions.
misconception: Using the field’s angle to the horizontal as its angle to the current.
transcription:
The figure shows a horizontal power cable of length $2.0\ \mathrm{m}$ carrying a steady current $I$ of $3.0\ \mathrm{A}$ into the plane of the paper.

[The current symbol is a cross in a circle. Earth’s magnetic field arrows point down and to the right in the plane of the paper, at $65^\circ$ to a dotted horizontal line.]

What is the force acting on the cable that is caused by the Earth’s magnetic field of flux density $4.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$, in a region where this field is at $65^\circ$ to the horizontal?

A $82\ \mathrm{\mu N}$
B $220\ \mathrm{\mu N}$
C $240\ \mathrm{\mu N}$
D $660\ \mathrm{\mu N}$

explanation.body: A neutral point occurs where the two magnetic flux densities are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. By the right-hand grip rule, the fields oppose each other only between the wires, in region 2.

perOption.B: The fields reinforce each other in both outer regions.
perOption.C: Changing the relative current magnitudes cannot reverse either field in an outer region.
perOption.D: The fields oppose each other in region 2 and can have equal magnitudes there.

difficultyReason: The right-hand grip rule identifies the region in which the two fields can cancel.
misconception: Assuming parallel currents produce fields in the same direction everywhere.

explanation.body: The two oppositely oriented diodes allow current through $R_1$ in both directions. One diode is in series with $R_2$, so the current in that direction has a smaller peak magnitude.

perOption.A: Shows equal peak magnitudes even though one direction adds $R_2$ in series.
perOption.B: Suppresses one half-cycle even though the second diode provides a path for it.
perOption.D: Shows both half-cycles with the same sign, although the current reverses through $R_1$.

issues: The supplied question PNG crops the lower parts of graphs C and D. The circuit and worked key establish that C represents alternating current with unequal peak magnitudes.
difficultyReason: The student must trace both half-cycles and compare the total series resistance in each direction.
misconception: Treating opposite diodes as a full-wave rectifier or as equal-resistance paths.
